content.page_title: Post-acute coronary syndrome pericarditis and Arrhythmias (excerpt)
content.summary: Describes pericardial complications after AMI and management of arrhythmias in the context of acute coronary syndromes (ACS), including atrial fibrillation (AF) and ventricular arrhythmias (VT/VF). Discusses timing of pericarditis, clinical significance of AF in ACS, and current acute management strategies for AF and malignant ventricular arrhythmias in STEMI/AMI.

12.2.4 Post-acute coronary syndrome peri.description: Pericardial complications after AMI include early infarct-associated pericarditis (few hours to 4 days after AMI, mostly transient), late pericarditis or post-cardiac injury (Dressler) syndrome (typically 1–2 weeks after AMI), and pericardial effusion.
12.2.4 Post-acute coronary syndrome peri.note: Topic discussed further in supplementary data online.

12.2.5 Arrhythmias.overview: Covers supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias occurring in ACS patients and recommended management principles.

12.2.5.1 Atrial fibrillation.description: AF is the most frequent supraventricular arrhythmia in patients with ACS. AF may be pre-existing, first detected, or new onset during ACS management. Patients with AF have more comorbidities and worse short- and long-term prognosis compared with patients in sinus rhythm.
management_recommendations: No specific treatment required in many cases apart from anticoagulation when indicated.
Prompt treatment required for AF causing acute haemodynamic instability: electrical cardioversion is preferred.
Adequate rate control can be achieved with beta-blockers, depending on presence of heart failure (HF) and reduced LVEF.
In patients with depressed LVEF, amiodarone or digoxin may be used (preferably amiodarone).
In hypotension, digoxin is preferred over amiodarone or beta-blockers.
Patients with AF and thrombo-embolism risk factors should receive appropriate chronic oral anticoagulation.
clinical_points: AF during STEMI that is transient and self-terminating may predict increased long-term stroke risk.
AF of any length in ACS is associated with worse outcomes.

12.2.5.2 Ventricular arrhythmias.description: With increased use of emergency reperfusion for STEMI, incidence of malignant ventricular arrhythmias (VT and VF) has declined, but a minority of patients still develop hemodynamically significant VT/VF.
12.2.5.2 Ventricular arrhythmias.epidemiology: Approximately 6–8% of patients with STEMI develop haemodynamically significant VT or VF.
management_recommendations: Urgent reperfusion is most important because ischaemia often triggers these arrhythmias.
Early administration of IV or oral beta-blockers reduces the incidence of malignant arrhythmias.
If malignant arrhythmias occur, beta-blockers or amiodarone are recommended; lidocaine may be considered if these are contraindicated.
12.2.5.2 Ventricular arrhythmias.prognosis: Prognostic role of early VT/VF within first 48 hours of STEMI is controversial; some studies suggest increased 30-day mortality but no increase in long-term arrhythmic risk.
